title: Helium was discovered on the Sun before it was found on Earth
body: During a total solar eclipse in August 1868, astronomers studying the Sun’s glowing outer layers with spectroscopes spotted a bright yellow line that didn’t match any known element. Norman Lockyer proposed it came from a new element and named it after Helios, the Greek word for the Sun. Helium wasn’t isolated on Earth until 1895, when William Ramsay and others found it seeping from a uranium mineral. It is now known to be the second most abundant element in the universe.

slides.heading: Which elements make up most of the ordinary matter in our galaxy, by mass?
slides.note: Spectroscopic estimate for the Milky Way. Everything else together is under 1%.
slides.explanation: Hydrogen and helium make up about 98% of it. Oxygen, carbon and neon come next, with iron close behind at 0.109%.

slides.question: How did astronomers first detect helium in 1868?
options: Gas seeping from a uranium mineral
A yellow line in the Sun’s spectrum
Bubbles in a balloon of hot air
Its glow inside a lightning bolt
slides.explanation: During the August 1868 total eclipse, spectroscopes showed a bright yellow line matching no known element. Lockyer named it after Helios, the Sun; it was found on Earth only in 1895.

slides.heading: Match each to its part in helium’s story
slides.explanation: A yellow line in the eclipse spectrum of 1868 matched no known element; Lockyer named it after the Sun, and Ramsay isolated it on Earth in 1895.
